strengths: Introduces OccuFly, the first real-world camera-only aerial 3D semantic scene completion (SSC) dataset, effectively filling a critical gap in a field heavily dominated by terrestrial autonomous driving datasets.

Proposes a highly efficient, LiDAR-free annotation pipeline that projects sparse 2D image annotations into a 3D reconstructed point cloud, requiring manual labeling of less than 10% of the images to achieve over 99% point coverage.

Includes a well-designed class-aware densification pipeline (using Poisson surface reconstruction for ground classes and silhouette-based voxel carving for instance classes) to generate high-quality volumetric ground truth from photogrammetry.
Offers extensive dataset variety spanning 9 scenes, multiple flight altitudes (30m, 40m, 50m), four seasons, and different scenario types (urban, industrial, rural) with a detailed 22-class taxonomy.
weaknesses: The benchmark evaluation for the Semantic Scene Completion task is limited to only one baseline model (CGFormer). Benchmarking additional representative SSC architectures (e.g., TPVFormer, VoxFormer, or MonoScene) would provide a more comprehensive overview of state-of-the-art performance on this new domain.

The photogrammetry-based label generation pipeline relies on standard SfM/MVS, which inherently assumes static scenes and cannot reliably handle dynamic objects (e.g., moving vehicles or pedestrians) common in real-world aerial scenarios.

The dataset suffers from extreme class imbalance (with the 'Building' class occupying over 75% of the dataset while several other classes are below 0.1%), resulting in extremely low overall mIoU during baseline evaluation. The paper would benefit from discussing strategies or standard baselines that employ class-balanced losses.

There is a lack of quantitative validation assessing the accuracy of the generated 'pseudo-ground-truth' against a high-fidelity reference (like a TLS scan or manual 3D labeling on a small subset) to measure how photogrammetric reconstruction artifacts propagate into the labels.

strengths: The paper introduces OccuFly, which is the first real-world, camera-based aerial Semantic Scene Completion (SSC) benchmark. This fills a significant gap, as existing SSC datasets are heavily dominated by ground-based autonomous driving scenarios.

The proposed camera-only data generation framework is practical and scalable. Utilizing Structure-from-Motion (SfM) and Multi-View Stereo (MVS) avoids the payload and energy constraints of LiDAR on UAVs, and the 2D-to-3D label projection reduces the annotation effort to labeling less than 10% of the images.
The dataset is large and diverse, providing over 20,000 samples across 9 scenes, 3 different altitudes (30m, 40m, 50m), multiple seasons, and a comprehensive 22-class taxonomy.
The paper is very well-written, with highly detailed explanations of the methodology and extensive qualitative and quantitative visualizations provided in the main text and supplementary material.
weaknesses: The performance of the benchmarked state-of-the-art model (CGFormer) is extremely low, yielding an overall mIoU of only 0.0080. While the authors state this highlights the difficulty of the aerial perspective, such an extremely low score (with many classes getting 0.0000 mIoU) raises concerns about whether the benchmark is currently too difficult or if the evaluation metrics are dominated by noise.

There is an extreme class imbalance in the dataset. As shown in Table 6, 'Building' alone accounts for 75.75% of the points, whereas most other classes (e.g., Person, Bicycle, Vehicles, Cables) represent less than 1% or even less than 0.01%. This severe skewness is likely the primary reason behind the exceptionally low mIoU and may limit the dataset's usefulness for learning fine-grained semantic representations.

The static scene assumption of the camera-only reconstruction pipeline means that dynamic objects (such as moving vehicles or pedestrians) cannot be properly captured or completed in 3D, which is a significant drawback for real-world UAV navigation and tracking applications.

The manual annotation effort, although reduced, still requires pixel-accurate labeling of approximately 10% of the images (amounting to nearly 600 high-resolution images as per Table 8). This remains non-trivial and time-consuming for 22 detailed classes.

Training the baseline model (CGFormer) on this dataset demands a massive amount of memory (32.39 GB peak memory for a batch size of 1 on an A100 GPU), which significantly restricts accessibility and reproducibility for researchers with limited computational resources.

strengths: Introduces the first real-world, camera-only aerial 3D Semantic Scene Completion (SSC) benchmark, which addresses a significant gap in visual perception for UAVs where heavy LiDAR sensors are restricted.

Proposes a highly efficient, LiDAR-free data generation framework that automates 3D label projection from sparse 2D annotations (requiring manually labeling less than 10% of frames), significantly lowering the high cost associated with 3D semantic labeling.

The dataset is large-scale, providing over 20,000 high-quality samples covering urban, industrial, and rural areas at multiple altitudes (30m, 40m, 50m) across four seasons, demonstrating high geographic and seasonal diversity.

Dual-utility of the dataset: alongside 3D SSC, it serves as a massive and dense metric monocular depth benchmark, containing 20,160 metric depth maps which vastly outscale existing aerial depth benchmarks.

The paper is very well-written, structurally sound, and provides extensive supplementary materials (detailed class statistics, visual comparisons, and implementation details) ensuring transparency and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The SfM-based reconstruction and label transfer assume static scenes, which inherently limits the dataset's ability to model truly dynamic moving objects.

The baseline evaluation of 3D SSC is somewhat limited, as it only benchmarks one model (CGFormer). Incorporating other state-of-the-art vision-based SSC methods (such as TPVFormer, MonoScene, or VoxFormer) would offer a more robust overview of the aerial domain's challenges.

There is a severe class imbalance in the dataset, with 'Building' accounting for over 75% of the voxel frequencies, while many critical classes (such as Vehicle, Person, or Truck) comprise less than 0.5%, which poses a massive challenge for effective training and evaluation on these minority categories.

strengths: Introduces the first real-world aerial Semantic Scene Completion (SSC) benchmark, filling an important gap in 3D scene understanding from an elevated/UAV perspective.
Proposes a highly scalable and cost-effective LiDAR-free data generation pipeline that leverages SfM/MVS reconstruction and lifts 2D annotations (<10% of images) to 3D, reducing annotation effort.
Provides a large-scale, diverse dataset with over 20,000 samples across multiple altitudes (30m, 40m, 50m), diverse environments (urban, industrial, rural), and four seasons.
Conducts thorough baseline evaluations for both SSC and monocular metric depth estimation, revealing clear limitations of current terrestrial and foundation models when applied to aerial views.
High-quality, detailed manuscript and supplementary material containing clear formulations, detailed statistics, and implementation details.
weaknesses: The performance of state-of-the-art SSC methods on the benchmark is extremely low (e.g., DISC achieves only 2.04% mIoU, and Symphonies achieves 0.58% mIoU). While this indicates a strong domain gap, it also raises questions about whether the benchmark is too difficult or if current models are entirely ill-suited without substantial architectural changes.

Extreme class imbalance in the dataset taxonomy (e.g., Buildings occupy 62.15% of voxel frequency, while classes like Person, Bicycle, and Cable are below 0.01%). This severe imbalance makes learning and evaluating rare classes highly challenging.
Reliance on classical SfM+MVS reconstruction for ground truth generation can introduce artifacts, especially on homogeneous surfaces, thin structures (cables, poles), and dynamic objects.

The dataset assumes static scenes, meaning dynamic objects might be misaligned or poorly reconstructed during multi-view aggregation, which restricts its applicability in highly dynamic real-world environments.

strengths: Highly Valuable Contribution: Introduces the first real-world camera-based aerial Semantic Scene Completion (SSC) benchmark (OccuFly), filling a significant gap in the 3D vision and UAV community where existing datasets are dominated by terrestrial driving settings.

Innovative and Cost-Effective Labeling Pipeline: Proposes an elegant 3D reconstruction and label-lifting framework that reduces the manual annotation effort. By annotating less than 10% of 2D images, the pipeline successfully labels over 99% of the reconstructed 3D points.

Large Scale and Rich Diversity: Contains more than 20,000 samples across 9 distinct scenes, capturing varied altitudes (30m, 40m, 50m), multiple seasons, and three different environment types (urban, rural, industrial). It also provides high-density metric depth maps.

Rigorous Benchmarking: The paper provides extensive experiments on both monocular depth estimation and SSC. It clearly demonstrates the limitations of current terrestrial foundation models and SSC methods when applied to the aerial domain.

Clarity and Quality of Presentation: The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with clear mathematical formulations, informative figures, and rich supplementary material detailing class distributions, implementation details, and scene visualizations.
weaknesses: Severe Class Imbalance: The class taxonomy (21 classes) is highly long-tailed. As shown in the supplementary material (Table 7), 'Building' accounts for over 62% of the dataset, while several classes (e.g., Person, Bicycle, Crane, Truck) have frequencies near zero (e.g., Person at 0.0001%). This extreme imbalance explains why the tested SSC models (Table 11) achieve near 0% IoU on almost all classes except 'Building' and a few ground classes, resulting in an extremely low mIoU (e.g., 2.04% for DISC).

Lack of Direct 3D Geometric Verification: The ground-truth is generated via classical SfM+MVS followed by silhouette carving (visual hulls) and Poisson surface reconstruction. While this is a creative way to bypass LiDAR, these reconstruction steps inevitably introduce geometric approximations (e.g., filling internal voids, smoothing sharp edges). Although 2D pixel-wise projection agreement is validated at 92%, a direct evaluation of the 3D geometric error of the voxelized grids against a high-accuracy ground-truth (like a terrestrial laser scanner or high-end aerial LiDAR) is missing.

Limitation to Static Scenes: Because SfM and MVS assume static environments, the pipeline cannot accurately reconstruct dynamic objects (such as moving vehicles or pedestrians). While acknowledged in the paper, this limitation restricts the dataset's utility for real-time dynamic UAV obstacle avoidance benchmarks.

Lack of Aerial-Specific Baselines or Adaptation: The paper benchmarks standard terrestrial SSC methods (Symphonies and DISC) and shows they perform very poorly. The contribution would be stronger if the authors proposed a baseline adaptation or simple modifications (e.g., incorporating pitch/roll aware projections or camera altitude priors) to show how to close this gap.

strengths: Introduces OccuFly, the first real-world camera-based aerial dataset and benchmark for 3D Semantic Scene Completion (SSC), addressing a key vacancy in low-altitude aerial scene understanding.

Proposes an efficient and scalable data generation framework that lifts 2D annotations from less than 10% of images into 3D using SfM+MVS, drastically reducing 3D annotation costs and bypassing the need for heavy aerial LiDAR.
The dataset is large and diverse, featuring over 20,000 samples with 21 semantic classes across various environments, seasons, and flight altitudes, as well as dense, high-quality metric depth maps.
Provides a thorough benchmark showing that existing vision foundation models and terrestrial SSC methods suffer from a severe domain gap, demonstrating the utility of OccuFly for future research.
weaknesses: The data generation pipeline relies on classical static 3D reconstruction, which suppresses truly dynamic objects and limits the dataset's applicability to highly dynamic environments.
The voxel resolution of 0.5m is relatively coarse, potentially missing fine-grained or thin aerial structures such as cables, tree branches, or small obstacles.

The SSC benchmarking is conducted on only two SOTA models (Symphonies and DISC); including older baselines or alternative representation types (like TPV-based methods) would provide a more comprehensive overview.
